threat_intel.summary: The current threat context for Hades Blackwatch centers on untrusted evidence flowing through agentic review pipelines, MCP/tool authority boundaries, skill and adapter supply-chain integrity, and governance-grade traceability. These signals are mapped to the local findings instead of being generic framework text.

signals.theme: Scanner and tool output is hostile evidence until minimized
signals.relevance: OWASP LLM guidance continues to emphasize sensitive information disclosure and improper output handling. For this repo, the practical risk is raw Burp, Qualys, Sonar, Semgrep, CodeQL, Trivy, or custom JSON evidence being copied into polished reports.
signals.recommended_action: Add recursive redaction before normalization and rendering, then make report generation tests assert that secrets never survive into HTML or PDF bytes.

signals.theme: MCP security depends on least privilege and precise authorization boundaries
signals.relevance: MCP security guidance calls out token passthrough, SSRF, local server compromise, session handling, and scope minimization. For Hades Blackwatch, this makes recursive manifest inspection and escalation-only MCP use important before connecting Burp, Qualys, Sonar, or internal scanners.
signals.recommended_action: Upgrade nested schema analysis, require risk-tier evidence for every MCP tool, and keep live MCP calls behind the necessity test.

signals.theme: Generated reports can become context poisoning in later agent runs
signals.relevance: Agentic systems are sensitive to stale or attacker-shaped context. The local surface mapper currently treats reports as review evidence, which can anchor later analysis on old findings and inflated keyword counts.
signals.recommended_action: Exclude generated report paths by default and require explicit opt-in when report artifacts themselves are the audit target.

signals.theme: Skill supply-chain integrity needs stable schemas and regression gates
signals.relevance: OWASP Agentic Skills and NIST AI RMF style governance both push toward provenance, traceability, and repeatable controls. Undocumented schema migration and manual-only smoke tests weaken downstream trust in this skill package.
signals.recommended_action: Document schema migration behavior and add automated tests plus CI before new adapters are added.

personalized_recommendations.why: Hades Blackwatch is becoming reusable security infrastructure. Redaction, schema naming, report rendering, generated-output exclusions, and recursive MCP checks should fail fast when changed.

findings.title: Raw scanner evidence can be copied into shareable HTML/PDF reports without secret redaction
findings.affected_component: scanner evidence normalization and report generation
findings.affected_asset: HTML/PDF security reports generated from scanner exports

evidence.summary: The generic normalizer assigns the entire scanner item to the normalized evidence field. The report generator then renders the evidence field into HTML and PDF. HTML escaping is present, but no recursive redaction or evidence minimization is applied before report generation.
observed_code_paths: render_html renders finding evidence through html_block
flatten_for_pdf serializes finding evidence into PDF text
evidence.positive_control: HTML content is escaped, reducing script injection risk. This does not prevent disclosure of sensitive scanner evidence.

findings.attack_path: A Burp, Qualys, Sonar, or custom scanner export includes request headers, cookies, bearer tokens, API keys, session identifiers, request bodies, or response snippets. normalize_findings.py copies the raw item into the evidence field. generate_report.py embeds that evidence in a polished report. The report is then shared more broadly than the raw scanner export, leaking sensitive operational details.
findings.ai_agent_relevance: The skill explicitly treats scanner output as untrusted input, and the report agent turns that input into downstream deliverables. In an agentic workflow, this expands the blast radius of sensitive scanner evidence unless redaction is deterministic.

threat_intel.summary: Current AI security guidance treats tool output, scanner output, and report artifacts as sensitive context that can leak credentials or operational details when copied without minimization.

sources.name: OWASP Top 10 for LLM and GenAI Apps 2025
sources.relevance: Sensitive information disclosure and improper output handling are directly relevant to report evidence leakage.

sources.name: NIST AI RMF Generative AI Profile

signals.relevance: Scanner exports commonly contain request headers, tokens, session values, response snippets, and internal hostnames.

framework_mappings.owasp_agentic: Information Disclosure through Tool and Context Handling
framework_mappings.mitre_atlas: Credential Access / Exfiltration through tool-output handling

score.rationale: The issue can expose high-value security evidence and credentials, is easy to reproduce with realistic scanner exports, and is amplified by automated report sharing.

findings.recommended_fix: Add a recursive redaction layer before storing normalized evidence and before rendering reports. Redact key names and values matching Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie, token, secret, password, api_key, bearer, private_key, session, credential, client_secret, and configurable organization patterns. Prefer a safe evidence summary allowlist over storing full raw scanner items by default.
findings.regression_test: Create a fixture with nested request and response objects containing Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie, api_key, password, bearer token, private key markers, and session IDs. Run normalize_findings.py and generate_report.py, then assert none of the secret values appear in normalized JSON, HTML, or PDF bytes.
findings.residual_risk: Some scanner proof data can remain sensitive even after key-based redaction. High-risk reports should carry a classification label and support an evidence-minimized mode.

findings.title: Surface mapper scans generated reports and previous report inputs, polluting later analysis
findings.affected_asset: review evidence quality and finding accuracy

evidence.summary: DEFAULT_SKIP_DIRS excludes common build and dependency folders but not reports/ or out/. The rerun included generated report HTML, PDF, and report input JSON as if they were source surfaces. The surface counts increased after report generation: mcp rose to 32, authz to 57, and secrets to 55 because prior reports contained those words.
evidence.control_gap: reports/ is ignored in .gitignore but not skipped by surface_mapper.py.

findings.attack_path: Generated reports contain security terminology and possibly sensitive evidence. A later full-stack analysis scans those reports and treats them as current code/docs evidence, producing duplicated findings, stale evidence, or false positives.
findings.ai_agent_relevance: Generated reports can become context for subsequent agent runs. If the tool cannot separate primary source from generated evidence, specialist agents may anchor on stale report content rather than current system behavior.

threat_intel.summary: Agentic review workflows are vulnerable to stale or attacker-shaped context when generated artifacts are re-ingested as if they were primary source evidence.

findings.residual_risk: Some users may intentionally want to audit report artifacts. That should be explicit and separate from source surface mapping.

findings.title: MCP manifest auditor can under-classify nested permissive tool schemas
findings.affected_asset: MCP risk tier assignment and tool safety classification

evidence.summary: The auditor reads only top-level schema properties for explicit issue generation. It may see nested words through JSON stringification, but it does not recursively report nested free-form parameters, unconstrained object schemas, additionalProperties, arrays of action objects, or weakly constrained nested URL/path/command/body fields.
evidence.positive_control: The example manifest correctly flags a top-level command parameter as T4.
evidence.gap: A tool can hide broad authority under a neutral top-level object such as config, request, options, action, or payload.

findings.attack_path: An MCP server exposes a tool with a benign top-level schema but nested command, URL, path, headers, body, credential, or action fields. The current auditor may not clearly emit high-risk nested JSON-path issues, causing the orchestrator to underestimate the server's risk tier.
findings.ai_agent_relevance: MCP tools are privileged agent boundaries. Under-classifying nested tool authority can make prompt injection or malicious tool metadata more dangerous in a connected agent environment.

threat_intel.summary: MCP security guidance emphasizes authorization boundaries, SSRF, token handling, local server risk, and scope minimization. Nested schemas can hide exactly the kind of authority that needs strict review.

signals.relevance: A neutral top-level object can contain nested command, URL, credential, body, or action fields that change the true risk tier.
signals.recommended_action: Walk schemas recursively and report exact JSON paths for risky nested fields and permissive object shapes.

threat_intel.detection_or_test: Add nested MCP manifest fixtures with command, URL, headers, body, credential, and additionalProperties paths; assert T4 classification.

framework_mappings.mitre_atlas: Tool abuse and execution via agent capability

score.rationale: The weakness affects detection quality for potentially high-risk tools. Impact depends on the reviewed MCP manifests and whether live high-privilege MCP tools are connected.

findings.recommended_fix: Walk input schemas recursively and report exact JSON paths. Flag additionalProperties true or absent on object-like inputs, nested sensitive parameter names, arrays of action objects, missing required fields, broad string parameters, and URL/path/command-like fields without enums, allowlists, regex constraints, or approval language.
findings.regression_test: Add a manifest fixture with inputSchema.properties.config.properties.command, inputSchema.properties.request.properties.url, nested headers/body fields, and additionalProperties true. Assert the auditor returns T4 and reports each nested JSON path.
findings.residual_risk: Static manifest checks cannot prove runtime authorization. High-risk MCP tools still need runtime review, allowlists, approval gates, and audit logs.

findings.title: Hades rename changed the normalized finding schema without compatibility notes
findings.affected_asset: normalized findings consumed by reports, CI, or downstream tooling

evidence.summary: normalize_findings.py now emits schema: hades-blackwatch.findings.v1 after the rename. Existing historical reports, dashboards, or downstream consumers may still expect a previous skill schema, but no compatibility note or alias is documented.
evidence.expected_output: schema: hades-blackwatch.findings.v1 with documented migration behavior for older consumers

findings.attack_path: Downstream systems or report consumers route, validate, or store findings based on the schema value. An undocumented schema migration can cause failed validation, incorrect ownership, broken dashboards, or mixed historical data after the skill rename.
findings.ai_agent_relevance: Agentic review workflows depend on machine-readable handoffs. Undocumented schema changes weaken provenance and can cause downstream agents or integrations to misinterpret the evidence source.

threat_intel.summary: Agentic security workflows rely on provenance, source identity, and repeatable machine-readable handoffs. Undocumented schema migrations reduce trust in downstream automation and audit evidence.

findings.title: Documentation describes scanner auto-detection before the registry implementation exists

evidence.summary: README and docs state that scanner backends are detected and that the skill chooses the safest integration path. The roadmap also says scanner_registry.py still needs to be added. The current implementation has a scanner-registry agent role but no executable scanner registry script.
evidence.current_implementation: Role guidance exists in agents/roles/scanner-registry.md, but scanner_registry.py is roadmap-only.
evidence.impact: Users may expect automatic detection of Sonar, Burp, Qualys, Semgrep, CodeQL, or Trivy when the current repo mainly supports manual/report-driven workflows.

findings.attack_path: A user relies on documentation that implies automated scanner detection, then assumes coverage exists when no scanner backend was actually queried or imported. This can create false assurance in a security review.
findings.ai_agent_relevance: Agentic tools should be explicit about what evidence was actually collected. Overstated capability descriptions can cause both humans and agents to over-trust missing scanner coverage.

threat_intel.summary: Threat-informed security reporting depends on evidence provenance. Overstating scanner or MCP coverage can create false assurance and hide missing controls.

findings.title: Smoke checks are manual and not enforced as automated regression tests
findings.affected_asset: future reliability of security review outputs

evidence.summary: Local smoke checks passed for skill validation, surface mapping, MCP manifest audit, prompt pack generation, normalization, and report generation. However, these checks are not codified as a test suite or CI gate.
successful_checks: generate_report.py produced HTML and PDF outputs
evidence.gap: No committed tests assert redaction, report generation, schema name, surface exclusion, nested MCP schemas, or PDF/HTML output integrity.

findings.attack_path: A future change regresses redaction, report escaping, schema names, surface exclusions, or MCP risk classification. Without automated tests, the regression may be discovered only after a report is shared or a review misses a risky tool.
findings.ai_agent_relevance: Security skills become reusable agent infrastructure. Regression in the skill can mislead future security reviews and downstream agent decisions.

threat_intel.summary: Reusable AI security skills become supply-chain components. Automated regression gates are needed so redaction, MCP risk classification, schema identity, and report rendering do not silently weaken over time.
